name: India
summary: Indian cuisine is a family of regional cuisines rather than one tradition. Spice blends, cooking fats, staple grains and vegetarian or non-vegetarian customs differ from state to state.
regional_variation: Climate, religion and trade shape what each region eats. The north leans on wheat breads, dairy and tandoor cooking. The south and east centre on rice, with coconut, tamarind or mustard depending on the coast. The west splits between vegetarian Gujarat and the seafood and coconut of the Konkan coast.

name: Italy
summary: Italian food is built on local ingredients and short ingredient lists. Many dishes belong to one town or province, and national unification only came in 1861.
regional_variation: The north cooks with butter, rice and polenta and makes fresh egg pasta. The south uses olive oil, dried durum-wheat pasta, tomatoes and strong flavours from the sea. Islands such as Sicily add Arab, Greek and Spanish influences.

name: Mexico
summary: Mexican cuisine rests on maize, beans and chiles, layered with Spanish, African and Asian ingredients since the 16th century. UNESCO lists traditional Mexican cuisine as intangible cultural heritage.
regional_variation: Oaxaca and Puebla are known for moles and indigenous ingredients. The Yucatan peninsula has a Maya base with Caribbean and Middle Eastern touches. Veracruz, on the Gulf coast, blends Spanish, African and Caribbean cooking and relies on seafood.

name: Morocco
summary: Moroccan cuisine blends Amazigh (Berber), Arab, Andalusian and Mediterranean traditions. It is known for slow-cooked tagines, steamed couscous, fragrant spice blends and a habit of mixing savoury and sweet. Bread, olives, preserved lemons and mint tea sit at the centre of everyday meals.
regional_variation: Morocco's food follows its geography. The imperial cities such as Fes and Marrakech hold refined court-style dishes, the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts cook fish and seafood, the mountains and the Sahara rely on grains, dates, argan and preserved meat, and the north carries Andalusian and Spanish echoes. Spice use, cooking fats and the choice of tagine or couscous shift from one area to the next.

name: Ethiopia
summary: Ethiopian cuisine is centred on injera, a sour fermented flatbread used as plate and spoon, and on spiced stews called wat. Chilli-rich berbere and spiced clarified butter give the food its depth. A strong tradition of fasting among Orthodox Christians has produced a large repertoire of vegan dishes.
regional_variation: Highland Amhara and Tigray cooking is built on teff injera and berbere-heavy wat, while the south uses enset, collards and more dairy, and Oromo cooking has its own traditions of butter, milk and coffee. Fasting days, which exclude meat and dairy, shape the weekly menu across much of the country, so the same people may eat very differently on a fasting day and a feast day. Meat dishes such as kitfo are linked to particular peoples such as the Gurage.

name: Egypt
summary: Egyptian cuisine is built on legumes, rice, bread and vegetables, with a long tradition of vegetarian dishes shaped partly by Coptic fasting. Fava beans, lentils, molokhia and stuffed vegetables are everyday food, and the Nile and the Mediterranean supply fish. Street food such as koshari and ta'ameya is central to city life.
regional_variation: Cairo and the Nile Delta are the country's food heartland, with rice, fava beans, molokhia and stuffed vegetables. Alexandria and the Mediterranean coast cook fish and seafood, while Upper Egypt and Nubia favour dates, grains, pigeon and sweeter spiced dishes, and Sinai Bedouin cooking centres on lamb, bread and the desert. Religious and seasonal calendars also shape what is eaten when.

name: Nigeria
summary: Nigerian cuisine is built on starchy staples such as yam, rice, cassava, millet and maize, eaten with richly seasoned soups and stews. Palm oil, hot peppers, fermented seasonings and dried fish or crayfish give many dishes their depth, and street grills and fried snacks are a big part of everyday eating.
regional_variation: Nigeria has hundreds of ethnic groups, and food differs with climate and tradition. The forested south relies on yam, palm oil and leafy soups, with Yoruba cooks favouring bean and pepper-based dishes and Igbo cooks emphasising yam and oil-rich soups. The coastal Niger Delta adds fish and palm fruit. The drier north is a grain and cattle region, where millet, sorghum, rice, milk and grilled meat feature more strongly.

name: South Africa
summary: South African cuisine blends indigenous African, Dutch, Malay, Indian and other influences, which is why it is often called a rainbow cuisine. Maize, beans, grilled and cured meats, spiced stews, curries and sweet baked puddings all sit side by side, and the braai (barbecue) is a social ritual across communities.
regional_variation: Food follows both geography and community. The Western Cape is known for Cape Malay spiced, lightly sweet dishes and Cape Dutch baking. KwaZulu-Natal has a large Indian-South-African community whose curries shaped Durban street food. The Nguni peoples of the east rely on maize, beans and fermented milk, while Afrikaner traditions centre on meat, sausages and pot cooking, and Johannesburg and the Highveld mix all of these in urban food.

name: China
summary: Chinese cuisine is a collection of regional traditions built around rice, wheat, soy products and a wide set of cooking techniques such as stir-frying, steaming, braising and roasting. Meals are usually shared, with several dishes eaten together alongside a staple of rice, noodles or bread.
regional_variation: Climate, geography and history split the country into distinct culinary regions. Sichuan is known for numbing and chilli heat, Guangdong for delicate steaming and roasting, and the lower Yangtze provinces for sweeter braises and fresh river produce. The north relies on wheat in the form of noodles, dumplings and buns, and the north-west of Xinjiang shares lamb, cumin and flatbreads with Central Asia.

name: Japan
summary: Japanese cuisine centres on rice, seafood, soy-based seasonings and seasonal produce, with dashi, miso and soy sauce providing much of the savoury depth. UNESCO has recognised washoku, the traditional dietary culture of the Japanese, as intangible cultural heritage.
regional_variation: A long north-to-south archipelago gives very different local foods. Hokkaido in the north is known for dairy, seafood and lamb, the Kanto and Kansai regions each have their own city food cultures and seasoning tastes, Kyushu favours richer, stronger flavours, and Okinawa has a distinct island cuisine shaped by its former Ryukyu Kingdom and its trade links.

name: Thailand
summary: Thai cooking balances sweet, sour, salty, hot and often bitter flavours within a single dish or across a shared meal. Rice is the staple, and meals typically combine a curry or soup, a stir-fry, a salad and dips with plenty of fresh herbs.
regional_variation: The central plains, with Bangkok, favour refined curries, coconut milk and royal-court influence. The north uses sticky rice, milder herb-driven dishes and Burmese and Yunnanese influences. Isan in the north-east has Lao-style sticky rice, grilled meats and sharp, spicy salads. The south uses fresh chillies, turmeric, seafood and spices from Malay and Muslim cooking.

name: Vietnam
summary: Vietnamese cooking emphasises fresh herbs, rice and rice noodles, fish sauce, and a balance of sweet, sour, salty and spicy flavours. Meals are lighter on oil and coconut than in many neighbouring cuisines, with plenty of raw greens and dipping sauces.
regional_variation: The north has a restrained, savoury style with noodle soups and Chinese influence. Central Vietnam, around Hue, is known for bold, spicy food and a tradition of small, refined imperial dishes. The south is sweeter, warmer and more abundant in herbs, fruit and coconut, reflecting its tropical climate and Mekong Delta produce.

name: France
summary: French cuisine is built on regional produce, technique and a strong culture of eating together. Butter, wine, cheese, bread and careful sauce-making are central, and each region has its own specialities. Its gastronomic meal is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
regional_variation: The north and west (Brittany, Normandy) use butter, cream, apples and seafood. Alsace and the east share Germanic influences such as sauerkraut and pork. Burgundy and the south-west are known for wine-based braises, beans and duck. Provence and the Mediterranean coast use olive oil, tomatoes, garlic, herbs and fish.

name: Germany
summary: German cuisine is hearty and strongly regional, built on pork, sausages, bread, potatoes, cabbage and preserved foods. Bread and baking traditions are especially rich, and many dishes are tied to the calendar of fairs, fasts and feasts.
regional_variation: Bavaria in the south favours roast meats, white sausages, pretzels and dumplings. Swabia is known for pasta-style dishes such as spätzle and Maultaschen. The Rhineland pairs sweet and sour in dishes like sauerbraten. Saxony and the east are known for baking, especially Christmas stollen. The north leans on fish, kale and pork.

name: Spain
summary: Spanish cooking is built on olive oil, garlic, tomatoes, pork, seafood, legumes and rice, shaped by Roman, Moorish and later New World influences. Meals are social, from shared tapas to long Sunday rice dishes, and the Mediterranean diet that Spain shares with several neighbours is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
regional_variation: Spain's regions have strong culinary identities. The Atlantic north (Galicia, the Basque Country) leans on seafood, salt cod and dairy. Catalonia and Valencia combine Mediterranean produce with rice and bread-based dishes. Andalusia in the south is the home of cold soups, fried fish and sweets with Arab-era roots, while the inland Castilian plateau favours roasts, bread soups and hearty stews.

name: Greece
summary: Greek cuisine centres on olive oil, vegetables, pulses, bread, cheese, lamb and fish, with herbs such as oregano and dill. It shares many dishes with its Balkan and eastern Mediterranean neighbours, and the Orthodox calendar of fasts and feasts shapes what is cooked through the year.
regional_variation: Crete is known for olive oil, wild greens and barley rusks. Macedonia and the north show Balkan and Ottoman-era influences, with pies, peppers and beans. The Aegean islands rely on pulses, capers, seafood and tomatoes grown in volcanic or dry soil, and mountainous Epirus is known for hand-rolled pies and sheep and goat dairy.

name: United States
summary: American food is a cuisine of immigrants and regions, built on Native American ingredients such as maize, squash, beans and turkey, and reshaped by British, African, German, Spanish, Italian, Asian and many other influences. Its best-known dishes are tied to places and to holidays, from New England chowder to Texas barbecue.
regional_variation: New England relies on seafood, dairy and maple. The South has a long tradition of frying, smoking and slow-cooked greens and pork, with a distinct Creole and Cajun cooking in Louisiana. The Midwest is shaped by dairy, grain and German and Scandinavian settlers, while the West Coast favours fresh produce, salmon and sourdough bread, and mixes in Asian and Latin American traditions.

name: Canada
summary: Canadian cuisine mixes the foods of Indigenous peoples, French and British settlers, and later waves of immigrants from Europe, Asia and elsewhere. Maple syrup, wheat, seafood, game and dairy are common threads, and many dishes are regional rather than national.
regional_variation: Quebec has a French-influenced cooking with strong maple, pork and dairy traditions. Atlantic Canada draws on the sea and on British and Irish customs, while Ontario combines farm produce with a large immigrant population. The Prairies are known for wheat, beef and the dishes of Ukrainian and other Central and Eastern European settlers, and British Columbia has salmon, seafood and strong Asian influences. Indigenous foods and techniques run through all regions.

name: Cuba
summary: Cuban cooking blends Spanish, West African and indigenous Taino traditions, with later touches from Caribbean neighbours and Chinese migrants. Pork, rice, beans, cassava and plantain are everyday staples, seasoned with garlic, cumin, oregano and sour orange rather than chile heat.
regional_variation: Differences are subtle rather than dramatic. The west, including Havana, is known for roast pork and garlicky mojo. Central Cuba is cattle, rice and sugar country. The east has stronger Caribbean and Haitian links, more coconut and cacao around Baracoa, and red beans cooked with rice in congrí.

name: Jamaica
summary: Jamaican cuisine combines West African, Taino, British, Spanish, Indian and Chinese influences. Allspice (pimento), scotch bonnet pepper, thyme and scallion season much of the cooking, and techniques such as jerking, curries, stewing and pickling sit alongside rice, ground provisions and coconut.
regional_variation: Differences follow parishes and heritage. Portland, in the north-east, is the home of jerk and Maroon traditions in the Blue Mountain foothills. St Elizabeth in the south-west is farming country known for provisions and roadside pepper shrimp. Kingston, the capital, is a meeting point of every influence, from Indian-style curries to patties and Chinese-Jamaican food.

name: Australia
summary: Australian cooking blends British colonial staples, waves of migrant cooking since the mid-20th century, and the much older foods of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Barbecues, bakery pies, seafood and sweet baking sit alongside a growing interest in native ingredients such as lemon myrtle and wattleseed.
regional_variation: A very large country with climates from tropical north to cool temperate south. The tropical north and Top End draw on barramundi, tropical fruit and rainforest plants; the temperate south-east leans on dairy, lamb, wheat and wine. Big cities such as Sydney and Melbourne are shaped by Greek, Italian, Chinese, Vietnamese and other migrant communities, while the outback has its own tradition of simple stockmen's food.

name: New Zealand
summary: New Zealand cooking combines Māori traditions, such as the hāngī earth oven, kūmara and kai moana (seafood), with British-style baking, roasts and pies brought by settlers. Lamb, dairy, seafood and fruit are high-quality local staples, and sweet baking such as pavlova and hokey pokey is closely identified with the country.
regional_variation: A long, narrow, mostly temperate country. The warm north grows kūmara and subtropical fruit and holds many Māori food traditions, Hawke's Bay is orchard and vineyard country, the West Coast is known for whitebait, and the cool south is known for oysters, lamb and hearty baking. Cities such as Auckland add Pacific, Asian and other migrant influences.

name: Fiji
summary: Fijian food draws on root crops such as dalo (taro) and cassava, coconut, reef fish and the earth-oven feast known as lovo. A second strand comes from the Indo-Fijian community, descended mainly from indentured labourers brought from India between 1879 and 1916, whose curries, dhal, roti and sweets are everyday food across the islands.
regional_variation: Viti Levu, the main island, holds the capital Suva and the western sugar and tourism belt, where Indo-Fijian cooking is strong. Vanua Levu to the north is more rural, with copra, cassava and a mix of Fijian and Indo-Fijian communities. The outlying Lau islands in the east are remote, with a food culture built on coconut, root crops and fish, and shaped by contact with nearby Tonga.

name: Samoa
summary: Samoan food is built on starchy crops such as taro, breadfruit and green bananas, fresh fish and coconut, cooked for centuries in the earth oven (umu). Everyday meals are simple, while feasts for church, family and village occasions are large and generous, in keeping with fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way.
regional_variation: Cooking varies less by region than by occasion and setting. The two main islands, Upolu and Savai'i, share the same core dishes. Urban Apia has bakeries, markets and a wider range of imported and Chinese-influenced foods, while village life on both islands stays closer to garden crops, reef fishing and the Sunday umu.

name: Tonga
summary: Tongan cuisine centres on root crops such as yam, taro and cassava, fresh fish and seafood, coconut and pork, much of it cooked in an earth oven (umu). Feasts are central to church, family and royal occasions and are laid out in large quantities, often with taro-leaf parcels called lu.
regional_variation: Tonga is made up of several island groups with different landscapes. Tongatapu is the main commercial centre and market hub, Vava'u and Ha'apai have a stronger fishing and subsistence tradition, and 'Eua's higher, wetter land is known for farming. The core dishes are shared across the kingdom, so differences lie mostly in what is grown, caught and sold locally.

name: Brazil
summary: Brazilian cuisine grew from the meeting of indigenous cassava and corn cooking, Portuguese techniques and African ingredients and skills brought by enslaved people, later joined by Italian, Japanese, German and Lebanese immigrants. Rice and beans are the everyday base, with cassava, corn, tropical fruit and a great deal of grilled meat.
regional_variation: The North-East, especially Bahia, uses coconut milk, dende palm oil and seafood in a strongly Afro-Brazilian style. Minas Gerais is known for cassava starch, cheese and pork. The South-East city of Sao Paulo is a melting pot of immigrant snacks, the South has a cattle-ranching grill culture, and the Amazon relies on river fish, tucupi and wild forest plants.

name: Peru
summary: Peruvian cuisine combines the produce of the Pacific coast, the Andes and the Amazon with indigenous, Spanish, African, Chinese and Japanese traditions. Potatoes, maize, ají chillies and fresh seafood are its backbone, and its raw-fish dishes and Chinese- and Japanese-influenced cooking are known worldwide.
regional_variation: The coast, centred on Lima, offers ceviche and the Chifa (Chinese-Peruvian) and Nikkei (Japanese-Peruvian) kitchens. The Andes rely on thousands of potato varieties, maize, freeze-dried tubers and earth-oven cooking. The Amazon uses river fish, plantain, cassava and leaf-wrapped rice and meat parcels.

name: Argentina
summary: Argentine cuisine is built on beef cooked over fire, wheat and corn, and the waves of Spanish and Italian immigration of the 19th and 20th centuries. Asado, empanadas, pasta and sweets filled with dulce de leche are everyday foods.
regional_variation: The Pampas around Buenos Aires are cattle country, home to asado and Italian-influenced dishes. The Andean North-West keeps indigenous corn, squash and bean traditions such as locro and humita. Cuyo, at the foot of the Andes, is wine and olive country, Patagonia is known for lamb and the Litoral for river fish and cassava starch dishes shared with Paraguay.

name: Colombia
summary: Colombian cuisine blends indigenous maize, potato and cassava with Spanish, African and some Middle Eastern influences. It is built on soups, corn arepas, plantain, rice and beans, with big regional differences from the Caribbean to the Andes.
regional_variation: Geography is the main divider. The Caribbean coast uses coconut, fish, cassava and fresh cheese; the Andean highlands favour potatoes, beans, pork and hearty soups; the Pacific coast cooks fish and shellfish with coconut and plantain; and the eastern plains are cattle country known for open-fire beef.

name: Chile
summary: Chilean food draws on a long coastline, fertile central valleys and a mix of indigenous Mapuche, Spanish and later European influences. Corn, potatoes, beans, seafood, beef and wine are staples, along with baked empanadas and fried breads.
regional_variation: Chile stretches over several climates. The arid north has desert oases and Andean products, the central valley is the agricultural heartland with corn, wine and market produce, and the south, including Chiloé, relies on potatoes, shellfish and smoked pork. Mapuche foods such as mote, merkén and piñones are important in the south.
